claim: A 2026 systematic evaluation built two independent allosteric-site benchmark subsets, including CAPASP-Unbound made of apo-state allosteric proteins.
quote: we created two independent datasets that had not been used in selected computational protocols: a CAPASP-General subset comprising holo state allosteric proteins and a CAPASP-Unbound subset comprising apo state allosteric proteins

claim: Machine-learning predictors PASSer and APOP led on sensitivity, F1 and MCC among five evaluated tools.
quote: the machine learning models PASSer and APOP, which are based on protein physicochemical properties, not only achieved the highest success rate in sensitivity prediction but also lead in average F1-score and MCC value

claim: Those same ML models degraded on the apo (unbound) subset relative to the holo subset, indicating an open gap for apo-only methods.
quote: these models performed better with the CAPASP-General subset than with the CAPASP-Unbound subset, suggesting that the prediction models require further improvement

claim: CorrSite2.0 uses the Gaussian network model to analyse motion correlations between allosteric and orthosteric sites, finding they are dominated by either fast or slow vibrational modes.
quote: we analyzed the dominant modes that determine motion correlations between allosteric and orthosteric sites using the Gaussian network model and found that motion correlations between allosteric and orthosteric sites are dominated by either fast or slow vibrational modes

claim: CorrSite2.0 scores candidate sites by taking the maximum of Z-scores computed separately from slow and from fast modes, reporting over 90% prediction accuracy.
quote: we developed CorrSite2.0 to predict allosteric sites by taking the maximum of the Z-scores calculated from using either slow or fast modes. The prediction accuracy of CorrSite2.0 outperformed other commonly used allosteric site prediction methods with prediction accuracy over 90.0%

claim: AlloEF (2026) is an ensemble allosteric-site model built on transfer entropy plus energetic features.
quote: AlloEF

claim: A 2023 method predicts allosteric pockets in protein biological assemblages.
quote: Predicting allosteric pockets in protein biological assemblages

claim: APOP predicts allosteric pockets by stiffening pairwise elastic-network interactions across a pocket to emulate ligand binding, then ranking pockets by the induced shift in global mode frequencies plus mean local hydrophobicity.
quote: we present APOP, a new allosteric pocket prediction method, which perturbs the pockets formed in the structure by stiffening pairwise interactions in the elastic network across the pocket, to emulate ligand binding. Ranking the pockets based on the shifts in the global mode frequencies, as well as their mean local hydrophobicities

claim: APOP places a known allosteric pocket in the top 3 for 92 of 104 test proteins.
quote: Out of the 104 test cases, APOP predicts known allosteric pockets for 92 within the top 3 rank

claim: AlloEF is a soft-voting ensemble of LightGBM, Random Forest and XGBoost integrating transfer-entropy dynamic features, energetic frustration, and sequence/structure/network-topology features.
quote: we develop AlloEF, an effective method for protein allosteric site prediction, which adopts a soft-voting classifier with LightGBM, Random Forest, and XGBoost combined. The multidimensional features are integrated, including the transfer entropy-based dynamic property and energetic frustration introduced by us

claim: Allo-Allo predicts allosteric sites from sequence alone using ESM-2 protein-language-model attention heads, reporting 67% higher AUPRC than prior state of the art.
quote: We introduce Allo-Allo, a data-efficient, sequence-based method that predicts allosteric sites by leveraging protein language models (PLMs). Honing in on ESM-2 attention heads that capture allosteric residue associations, Allo-Allo achieves a 67% higher AUPRC than state-of-the-art methods.

claim: ASBench provides benchmarking sets of experimentally determined allosteric sites: a Core set of 235 unique sites and a Core-Diversity set of 147 structurally diverse sites.
quote: including a ‘Core set’ with 235 unique allosteric sites and a ‘Core-Diversity set’ with 147 structurally diverse allosteric sites

claim: The Allosteric Database (ASD) was introduced as a central online resource for allosteric molecules, initially holding 336 allosteric proteins from 101 species and 8095 modulators.
quote: ASD contains 336 allosteric proteins from 101 species and 8095 modulators in three categories (activators, inhibitors and regulators)

claim: KeyAlloSite predicts allosteric sites and key allosteric residues from evolutionary coupling rather than structure dynamics.
quote: we developed a novel computational method KeyAlloSite to predict allosteric site and to identify key allosteric residues (allo-residues) based on the evolutionary coupl

claim: A 2025 review frames allosteric drug discovery as converging on three computational approaches -- machine learning, MD simulation, and network theory -- with network analyses supplying communication pathways for site identification.
quote: driven by the integration of three computational approaches: machine learning (ML), molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and network theory

claim: The same review names generalizability and limited datasets as persisting challenges in the field.
quote: However, challenges like high computational costs, limited datasets, and model generalizability persist.

claim: Using the adjacency matrix instead of the graph Laplacian as the CTQW generator gives an identical walk only on regular graphs; on non-regular graphs the two are genuinely inequivalent quantum walks.
quote:
While this is equivalent to the Laplacian for
regular graphs, it is diﬀerent for non-regular graphs, and is thus an inequiv-
alent quantum walk.

claim: The reason regularity collapses the distinction is that for a regular graph the degree matrix is proportional to the identity, so it contributes only an unobservable global phase and can be dropped.
quote:
If the graph is regular, then the degree matrix D is a multiple of the identity
matrix, so it only constitutes an unobservable, global phase or a rezeroing
of energy and can be dropped [5].

claim: On a non-regular graph the Laplacian and adjacency walks differ in four concrete respects: the required jumping rate, the runtime, which marked vertices get sampled, and what counts as a natural initial state.
quote:
The two walks diﬀer qualitatively
and quantitatively in their required jumping rate, runtime, sampling of marked
vertices, and in what constitutes a natural initial state.

claim: The uniform superposition is a zero-eigenvalue eigenvector of the Laplacian (hence stationary under the Laplacian walk) but is not an eigenvector of the adjacency matrix, so an adjacency-generated walk makes the uniform state drift even with no external driving.
quote:
The equal superposition |s⟩, however, is not an eigenvector of A. Then the
quantum walk governed by the adjacency matrix alone (i.e., H = −γA), will
cause |s⟩to evolve, even though no oracle is being queried and our information
is unchanged.

claim: For an adjacency-matrix walk the natural initial state is instead a degree-dependent, non-uniform superposition that is an eigenstate of A, so that the walk alone leaves the probability distribution unchanged.
quote:
which is an eigenstate of A with eigenvalue √N1N2. With this state, vertices in
the left vertex set start with probability 1/2N1, and vertices in the right vertex
set start with probability 1/2N2.

claim: The Laplacian walk on the non-regular bipartite graph localizes the outcome entirely within one degree class (one vertex set) depending on the jumping rate, whereas the adjacency walk samples both vertex sets simultaneously.
quote:
Thus depending on whether γ equals γa or γb, the system evolves to one
of |a⟩or |b⟩, not a combination of |a⟩and |b⟩. That is, the ﬁnal state samples
entirely from the marked vertices in one vertex set or the other.

claim: In the worked example with N1=512, N2=256, k1=3, k2=5 the adjacency walk splits its final probability unequally but proportionally to the degree/marked-vertex structure, reaching 0.231 in one set and 0.769 in the other for total success probability 1.
quote:
the probability in |a⟩reaches 3·256/(5·512+3·256) ≈0.231, and the probability
in |b⟩reaches 5 · 512/(5 · 512 + 3 · 256) ≈0.769, for a total success probability
of 1.

claim: Neither generator dominates: which of the Laplacian or adjacency walk is faster depends on the distribution of marked and unmarked vertices, so the generator choice is a real algorithmic design decision rather than a convention.
quote:
the runtimes of the respective algorithms are, in gen-
eral, diﬀerent, and depending on the number of marked and unmarked vertices
in each vertex set, one walk can outperform the other.

claim: The standard CTQW construction identifies the quantum Hamiltonian with the negative of the classical CTRW transfer matrix, which is what lets coherent and incoherent transport be compared on exactly the same network topology.
quote:
One can push the similarities further by identifying the
quantum-mechanical Hamiltonian H with the classical trans-
fer matrix T , i.e., H ≡−T . This approach, pioneered by
Farhi and Gutmann in Ref. [21], allows to compare the two
extremes of transport on the same topology.

claim: The 'connectivity matrix' A used as the CTQW generator in this review is exactly the graph Laplacian (node degree on the diagonal, -1 for connected pairs), and it is real symmetric with non-negative eigenvalues and a single zero eigenvalue.
quote:
where fj is the number of bonds emanating from node j. This
matrix has interesting and useful properties: (a) A is real and
symmetric, (b) all its eigenvalues λn are real and λn ≥0, and
(c) A has a single smallest eigenvalue which is λ1 = 0.

claim: Because unitary CTQW evolution has no unique long-time limit, the standard observable is the infinite-time (long-time) average of the transfer probability, which still retains dependence on both the initial and final node.
quote:
Unlike the situation for CTRW, for CTQW there is no unique
long-time limit of πk,j(t) due to the unitary time evolution. In
order to compare to the long-time behavior of the CTRW one
uses the long time average [70, 71]

claim: The infinite-time average reduces to a sum restricted to degenerate eigenvalue pairs, so eigenvalue degeneracy (a symmetry property of the graph) is what determines the long-time transfer probability, and it also makes the quantity cheap to compute from the spectral decomposition.
quote:
One notes that the integral in Eq.(46a) equals 1 if λn = λm
and 0 otherwise, i.e., it equals δλn,λm. Given that some eigen-
values of H are degenerate, the sum in Eq.(46b) can contain
terms belonging to different eigenstates |qn⟩and |qm⟩.

claim: The classical CTRW baseline is topology-blind at long times: every CTRW whose transfer matrix comes from the connectivity matrix relaxes to the equipartition value 1/N regardless of network structure.
quote:
Therefore, the long-time limit of all transition probabilities is
limt→∞pk,j(t) = 1/N, which is independent of the connec-
tivity of the network.

claim: In contrast to the classical case, the CTQW long-time average is not equipartitioned but retains memory of the starting node, so it carries structural information that the classical diffusion limit destroys.
quote:
Thus, unlike in the classical CTRW case the long-time average
is not equipartitioned but “remembers” the initial condition.

claim: On a strongly degree-heterogeneous graph (a star with one hub and many peripheral nodes) the coherent CTQW performs far worse than the classical walk: return probability stays near unity so the walker rarely leaves its starting node, and the poor performance comes from the many peripheral (low-degree) starting nodes.
quote:
The contrary is true for the star. Here, the CTRW still decay
while the CTQW remain close to unity. This implies that the
probability to visit other places than the initial node is - on
average - very low.

claim: On random scale-free networks (power-law degree distribution) the ensemble-averaged CTQW return probability saturates at a stationary value about an order of magnitude above the classical equipartition value 1/N, and that value grows with the symmetry of the starting node.
quote:
In the ensem-
ble average the return probabilities do not oscillate but rather
reach a stationary value, which differs for different initial
nodes. In all cases, however, this stationary value is roughly
one order of magnitude larger than the classical equipartition
value 1/N obtained for CTRW.

claim: Environmental noise can increase rather than degrade excitation transport through an interacting network, the effect termed environment-assisted quantum transport (ENAQT).
quote:
Remarkably, environmental noise can
enhance the transport, an eﬀect known as environment-assisted quantum transport (ENAQT).

claim: Sweeping dephasing strength in a 10-qubit network produces a three-regime crossover: coherent dynamics with Anderson localization at low noise, ENAQT-enhanced transport at intermediate noise, and Zeno-suppressed transport at high noise.
quote:
With increasing noise strength, we observe a crossover from coherent dynamics and
Anderson localization to ENAQT and ﬁnally a suppression of transport due to the quantum Zeno
eﬀect.

claim: The optimum dephasing rate sits where the noise rate matches the hopping scale (gamma approximately Jmax); there the noise cancels the destructive interference that causes localization and maximizes transport efficiency.
quote:
At
weak dephasing, γ < Jmax, excitation transport is sup-
pressed corresponding to Anderson localization. Around
γ ≈Jmax, the noise cancels destructive interference caus-
ing the localization and thereby enhances the transport
eﬃciency, which is the hallmark of ENAQT.

claim: Localization in the coherent walk is a wave-interference effect, and dephasing works by destroying that destructive interference, which is why adding noise unblocks transport.
quote:
This
highlights the fact that Anderson localization is a wave
phenomenon caused by destructive interference, which is
lifted by dephasing.

claim: Fitting the wave-packet width to a power law shows transport is near-ballistic at the ENAQT optimum (exponent 0.76 +/- 0.18) but becomes subdiffusive under strong dephasing at gamma = 18.4 Jmax (exponent 0.44 +/- 0.02).
quote:

with a power exponent C = 0.44 ± 0.02.

claim: Structured non-Markovian noise can match white-noise transport efficiency at roughly half the injected energy cost, and preserves coherences better, so the spectral shape of the environment, not just its strength, is a tunable design parameter.
quote:
we ﬁnd that with narrowband
non-Markovian noise we can achieve similar transport ef-
ﬁciencies as with Markovian noise, but already at half the
energy cost (cf. noise models 1 and 6 in Fig. 4 (a)).

claim: PASSer takes only a PDB ID or user-uploaded PDB file and requires an explicit geometry-based pocket-detection step (FPocket) before any machine learning model scores the candidate sites.
quote: FPocket, a geometry-based pocket detection package ( 25 ), is then used to detect potential protein pockets in the resulting protein structure ( 25 ). The user-selected machine learning model is applied for the prediction of detected pockets.

claim: The ensemble model combines XGBoost trained on 19 FPocket physicochemical pocket features with a graph convolutional network operating on a per-pocket atomic graph, averaging the two probabilities.
quote: In the ensemble learning method, XGBoost ( 20 ) learns 19 physical and chemical features calculated by FPocket. GCNN ( 26 ) builds an atomic graph for each pocket to learn the local connectivity at atomic level.

claim: The learning-to-rank model scores pockets relative to each other within a single protein rather than assigning absolute probabilities, outputting a rank score per pocket.
quote: For the learning-to-rank model, all pockets in a given protein are ranked with regard to their relevance of being allosteric sites.

claim: The third PASSer model is a LambdaRank-objective boosted-tree ranker implemented on LightGBM.
quote: a learning-to-rank model with the boosted tree version of LambdaRank objective on LightGBM ( 16 ).

claim: Reported PASSer accuracies are top-1 60.7% / top-3 84.9% (ensemble), top-1 65.1% / top-3 82.7% (AutoML) and top-1 59.5% / top-3 83.6% (learning-to-rank), with F1 scores of 0.782, 0.701 and 0.662.
quote: F 1 score Top 1 Top 3 Ensemble learning 0.726 0.847 0.782 60.7% 84.9% Automated machine learning 0.850 0.616 0.701 65.1% 82.7% Learning-to-rank 0.662 0.662 0.662 59.5% 83.6%

claim: After filtering ASD (1949 entries) for resolution, completeness and 30% sequence identity plus a 10 A modulator-pocket distance cutoff, only 207 proteins remained as training data.
quote: Through the data cleaning steps above, 207 proteins were included to train machine learning models.

claim: The authors caution that the three models' reported numbers are not directly comparable because each was trained and tested on different datasets.
quote: It is important to note that performance is not directly comparable across models due to differences in the training and test datasets used.

claim: The LambdaMART learning-to-rank model placed a true allosteric pocket in its top 3 for 83.6% of ASD test proteins and 80.5% of CASBench proteins.
quote: allosteric pocket in the top 3 positions for 83.6% and 80.5% of test proteins, respectively.

claim: The ranking algorithm is LambdaMART, i.e. gradient-boosted decision trees trained with the lambdarank loss that directly optimizes NDCG over the candidate list.
quote: In this study, we implemented the LTR algorithm using GBDT and the LambdaMART

claim: Input is a single static structure processed by FPocket, giving on average 21 pockets per protein (4413 pockets over 207 proteins), each described by only 19 physicochemical features.
quote: in each protein, with a total of 4413 pockets in 207 proteins. For each detected pocket, 19

claim: Ground-truth labels are generated automatically by assigning the pocket whose center of mass is closest to the bound modulator as the positive allosteric site.
quote: by assigning the closest pockets to the modulator as the allosteric site. The center of mass is

claim: On the held-out ASD test set LambdaMART beat XGBoost, random forest, SVM and raw FPocket scoring in 8 of 9 evaluation metrics.
quote: achieved the best performance in 8 out of 9 metrics among all models.

claim: On the external CASBench set performance dropped but LambdaMART still led FPocket in 7 of 9 metrics.
quote: and leads in 7 out of 9 metrics.

claim: SHAP analysis showed the FPocket druggability score itself dominates feature importance, i.e. the learned ranker leans heavily on one geometric pocket score.
quote: The results indicate that the FPocket score was the most important

claim: A stated data-preparation limitation is that proteins carrying multiple modulators in the same chain are discarded, since they break the one-positive-pocket-per-protein assumption.
quote: proteins with multiple modulators in the same chain are discarded

claim: STINGAllo is residue-centric: it classifies every residue as allosteric-site-forming using 54 optimized internal-protein-nanoenvironment descriptors, giving single-residue resolution instead of pocket scores.
quote: Using 54 optimized internal protein nanoenvironment descriptors, STINGAllo predicts allosteric site-forming residues at single-residue resolution.

claim: STINGAllo reports 78% success on benchmark data and a 60.2% overall success rate versus 21.1%-24.2% for pocket-based predictors.
quote: It achieves a success rate of 78% on benchmark datasets, substantially outperforming existing methods with a 60.2% overall success rate compared with 21.1%–24.2% for contemporary pocket-based predictors.

claim: The per-residue features combine hydrophobic interaction networks, local density, graph connectivity and a sponge-effect metric, letting the model score residues without any surface-geometry or pocket-detection step.
quote: By integrating hydrophobic interaction networks, local density, graph connectivity, and a unique “sponge effect” metric, STINGAllo detects allosteric sites independently of surface geometry, including concave pockets, flat surfaces, or even cryptic regions.

claim: The predictor is a CatBoost gradient-boosted decision tree over more than 1200 per-residue structural and physicochemical descriptors of the internal protein nanoenvironment.
quote: The core of the predictor is a CatBoost gradient-boosted decision tree model, which was trained and validated as detailed in our previous work [ 12 ]. The model leverages a rich feature set of over 1200 structural and physicochemical descriptors that characterize the IPN of each residue.
section: Materials and methods (The STINGAllo prediction model)

claim: Input is a single static structure only: an uploaded PDB file triggers de novo computation of over 1200 IPN descriptors per residue, with no MD trajectory or sequence alignment required.
quote: It then initiates a de novo calculation pipeline to generate the complete set of over 1200 IPN descriptors for each residue. This feature matrix is then used for prediction.
section: Materials and methods (Input processing and prediction workflow)

claim: Benchmarking used an independent 91-protein-chain test set drawn from ASBench and excluded from training.
quote: The benchmark was conducted on an independent test set of 91 protein chains from the ASBench database, which were not used during model training.

claim: Success is measured by the DCC criterion: the geometric center of the predicted residue cluster must lie within 4 A of the center of the experimentally known allosteric site.
quote: The primary metric for comparison was the DCC success rate, which measures whether the geometric center of the predicted AFRs is within 4 Å of the center of the experimentally known allosteric site.

claim: A stated limitation is training-set bias: ASBench is dominated by globular enzymes and small soluble signaling proteins, so membrane, multimeric and IDR-rich systems are essentially unrepresented and predictions there are unvalidated.
quote: The dataset is dominated by globular enzymes and small soluble signaling proteins, accounting for the vast majority of ASBench entries, while membrane-embedded, multimeric, or intrinsically disordered region (IDR)-rich systems are largely absent

claim: PocketMiner is a graph neural network trained on MD pocket-opening events that scores cryptic-pocket formation from a single input structure, reaching ROC-AUC 0.87 on a curated set of 39 confirmed cryptic pockets while being >1,000-fold faster than prior methods.
quote: Applying PocketMiner to single structures from a newly curated dataset of 39 experimentally confirmed cryptic pockets demonstrates that it accurately identifies cryptic pockets (ROC-AUC: 0.87) >1,000-fold faster than existing methods.

claim: The PocketMiner GNN input graph uses only backbone geometry: per-residue node features are backbone dihedrals plus forward/reverse unit vectors, and edge features are a radial-basis encoding of inter-residue distance plus the unit vector between alpha-carbons.
quote: Node features include backbone dihedral angles as well as forward and reverse unit vectors (for a full list see Methods). Edge features include a radial basis encoding of the distance between residues and a unit vector between their alpha-carbons.

claim: Training labels were generated automatically from MD: each residue in a 40 ns window's starting structure is labelled positive if it participates in a cryptic pocket at any point in the following 40 ns, over a dataset of 37 proteins and 2400 independent simulations.
quote: This dataset included 37 proteins and 2400 independent MD simulations at least 40 ns in length. We generated labels for each residue in each 40 ns window’s starting structure based on whether that residue participates in a cryptic pocket

claim: The simulation-label training set contained 941,650 unique residue examples, which the authors used to train a geometric-vector-perceptron graph neural network.
quote: Altogether, this dataset included 941,650 unique examples.

claim: In 5-fold protein-level cross-validation on the simulation task the GVP-GNN reached mean test PR-AUC 0.44 and ROC-AUC 0.83, slightly ahead of a 3D convolutional neural network baseline.
quote: Across the 5 splits, the best GVP-GNN model achieves an average test PR-AUC of 0.44 ± 0.12 (average ROC-AUC: 0.83 ± 0.04; Fig.  4B–C ). The 3D-CNN performs similarly (PR-AUC: 0.41 ± 0.05; ROC-AUC: 0.79 ± 0.02).

claim: The competing CryptoSite predictor needs on-the-fly simulation data as an input feature (about one day per protein) and loses accuracy when that feature is dropped, falling from ROC-AUC 0.83 to 0.74.
quote: Achieving this performance requires ~1 day to run for a single protein because one of CryptoSite’s input features is simulation data, which it needs to generate on-the-fly for each prediction. The algorithm takes a performance hit without using simulation data as a feature (ROC-AUC = 0.74).

claim: PocketMiner's held-out evaluation set is small and mixes positives and curated negatives: 24 apo structures with ligand-binding cryptic pockets, 4 hyper-rigid proteins and 7 extensively ligand-screened proteins, and it beat CryptoSite 0.87 vs 0.85 ROC-AUC.
quote: When we compared the performance of our model against CryptoSite, we find that the two methods give very similar performance, with PocketMiner providing a small advantage (ROC-AUC: 0.87 for PocketMiner vs. 0.85 for CryptoSite).

claim: For protein-level screening the residue scores are aggregated into a hotspot score (a residue plus its 10 neighbours); thresholding that score at 0.7 gave 0.90 accuracy, correctly classifying 21/24 positives and 3/4 negatives.
quote: At a threshold of 0.7, we achieve an accuracy of 0.90 with 3/4 negative examples correctly identified and 21/24 positive examples correctly identified.

claim: AlloPred's core algorithm perturbs an elastic-network normal-mode model by stiffening the springs of residues in a candidate pocket and measures the resulting change at the active site, i.e. it needs only a structure plus active-site residue indices.
quote:
The normal
modes of the protein were then calculated using the elas-
tic network model, except the spring constant of any atom
pair including a residue in a chosen pocket was set to be
a higher value. The effect of this perturbation was mea-
sured at the active site.

claim: The paper argues normal mode analysis captures protein dynamics well enough for allostery even at coarse resolution, explicitly noting that considering only C-alpha atoms can be sufficient.
quote:
NMA is effective at describing
protein dynamics, despite ignoring the complex nature of
the protein energy landscape [24]. Even considering the
C-alpha atoms alone can be sufficient.

claim: After chi-squared ranking of 65 candidate features only 7 were retained, and the most informative ones mix pocket geometry with normal-mode perturbation scores and the distance from the pocket to the active site.
quote:
The retained features,
in descending order of descriptive power, were:
• Number of alpha spheres (raw)
• E200 (ranked)
• Score (raw)
• Eall (ranked)
• Distance to active site (raw)
• Pocket size (raw)
• Fpocket rank (raw)

claim: Pocket candidates come from a separate Fpocket detection step using Voronoi tessellation and alpha spheres, and the SVM ranks those pockets, so the method depends on an all-atom pocket detector rather than raw residue coordinates.
quote:
Pockets on the protein were first predicted
using the Fpocket algorithm [26], which locates pockets
using Voronoi tessellation and alpha spheres.

claim: AlloPred's benchmark derives from the ASBench Core-Diversity set of 147 allosteric sites on 127 proteins, reduced to 119 usable proteins and split into 79 training and 40 test proteins.
quote:
This left 119 proteins in the dataset. The dataset was ran-
domly split into a training set of 79 proteins and a test set
of 40 proteins.

claim: On the 40-protein test set AlloPred ranked an allosteric pocket first for 23 proteins (against an 18% base rate of allosteric pockets) and first or second for 28 proteins.
quote:
For 23 of 40 proteins
AlloPred ranked top a pocket containing an allosteric
binding residue (an allosteric pocket), when 18 % of pock-
ets were allosteric pockets. For 28 of 40 proteins an
allosteric pocket was ranked first or second.

claim: On the same test set the pocket-descriptor-only AlloSite ranked an allosteric pocket top in 21 of 40 cases while the flexibility-plus-conservation method PARS did so in only 10 of 40, and AlloPred made 4 correct predictions neither method made.
quote:
PARS ranked an allosteric
pocket top in 10 of 40 cases. Figure 3 shows that Allo-
Pred compares well to other methods and makes 4 correct
predictions that neither of the other methods do.

claim: The stated main limitation is mechanistic: a method built on changes in dynamics upon ligand binding misses allostery arising from oligomer rigid-body motion, side-chain dynamics or local unfolding, and is unsuitable for cases like haemoglobin.
quote:
The main limitation of our method is related to the
diversity found in allosteric systems. Rigid-body motions
of oligomers, side-chain dynamics, backbone motions
and local unfolding are all mechanisms of allostery

claim: CASBench is a benchmark of 91 enzyme entries that carry both catalytic and allosteric site annotations in their structures, compiled from the Allosteric Database, Catalytic Site Atlas and PDB.
quote:
The CASBench benchmark set 
contains 91 entries related to enzymes with both catalytic and allosteric sites within their structures annotated 
based on the experimental information from the Allosteric Database, Catalytic Site Atlas, and Protein Data 
Bank.

claim: The authors explicitly intend CASBench as an evaluation and training resource for algorithms that search for catalytic and regulatory sites, i.e. it is usable as a held-out test set.
quote:
The obtained dataset can be used to benchmark the performance of existing computational approaches 
and develop/train perspective algorithms to search for new catalytic and regulatory sites

claim: Because every CASBench protein carries annotations for both site types, the set is explicitly offered as training data for algorithms that must learn to recognize and distinguish catalytic from allosteric sites.
quote:
The availability of annotations for both sites in each 
protein provides an opportunity to study the organi­
zation of sites of different types and to train computer 
algorithms to recognize them.

claim: In every CASBench entry the catalytic and allosteric sites are topologically separate cavities; in 30% of cases they overlap or share a border and in 70% they are far apart, which matters for whether an active-site-seeded ranking model can separate them.
quote:
In 30% 
of cases, the catalytic and allosteric sites either overlap 
or share a common border; in 70% of entries, both sites 
reside at a considerable distance from each other and 
do not overlap within the structure.

claim: Unlike the raw ASD/CSA annotations, which may list only a few experimentally verified residues, CASBench site definitions are expanded using crystallographic complexes so that all residues directly contacting ligands are listed, giving explicit site boundaries.
quote:
the annotations of sites 
from the ASD and CSA databases are refined using 
the information from the crystallographic complexes 
of proteins with ligands. All residues directly inter­
acting with ligands are shown in the benchmark set,

claim: The source ASD database holds nearly two thousand allosteric entries but is redundant and poorly annotated, with only about 235 entries usable in practice for training or evaluating algorithms, and it carries no catalytic-site annotation.
quote:
The ASD database is an important re­
source on allosteric proteins but contains redundant 
(duplicated) data and low-quality annotations; so, 
only a small part of this collection can be used in 
practice to study allostery and train/evaluate new 
algorithms (235 entries [41]).

claim: The paper's stated limitation of existing site-search algorithms is that they detect pockets and rank them by an evaluation function without distinguishing catalytic from allosteric sites, so they cannot discriminate between site types.
quote:
We 
can also note the common limitation of the known 
search algorithms: they do not take into account the 
differences between the functional (catalytic) and 
regulatory (allosteric) sites and, therefore, are unable 
to discriminate between sites of different types.

claim: Each CASBench entry also ships a multiple sequence alignment of a representative family set in FASTA, intended for testing algorithms that use bioinformatic (conservation) analysis to find or rank ligand binding sites.

claim: Bond-to-bond propensity analysis predicts allosteric sites from an energy-weighted atomistic graph built from a single protein structure, requiring knowledge only of the location of the active site.
quote:
A recently developed method, bond-to-bond propensity analysis, has proven 
capable of predicting allosteric sites in a wide range of proteins using an energy-weighted atomistic 
graph obtained from the protein structure and given knowledge only of the location of the active site.

claim: Stated limitation of coarse-graining: the authors argue modelling at the individual bond level matters because coarse-graining even to the residue level may remove crucial information.
quote:

claim: Benchmarked on 432 structures of 146 proteins from ASBench and CASBench, bond-to-bond propensity recovered the allosteric site for 127 of 146 proteins (407 of 432 structures) using only knowledge of the orthosteric sites or ligands.
quote: The allosteric site is recovered for 127 of 146 proteins (407 of 432 structures) knowing only the orthosteric sites or ligands.

claim: On ASBench, with the allosteric ligand removed so that only orthosteric site residues seed the perturbation, allosteric sites were still identified for 84% of the structures.
quote: Despite a lower success rate without the allosteric ligand, allosteric sites of 84% of the structures can be identified with only the knowledge of orthosteric site residues.

claim: On CASBench (314 structures of 33 proteins) the allosteric site was detected by at least one statistical measure for 308/314 (98.1%) structures when seeding from orthosteric ligands and 304/314 (96.8%) when seeding from orthosteric site residues, covering 32 of 33 proteins in both cases.
quote: managed to detect the allosteric sites according to at least one statistical measure for 308 of 314 (98.1%) structures (32 of 33 proteins) and for 304 of 314 (96.8%) structures (32 of 33 proteins), respectively.

claim: Reported prediction accuracies of competing benchmarked methods are 51.7% for AllositePro, 59% for AlloPred and 65% for PARS, all below the 84% reported for bond-to-bond propensity on ASBench.
quote: The prediction accuracies of AllositePro, 51 AlloPred, 50 and PARS 48 are 51.7%, 59%, and 65%, respectively

claim: Method families for allosteric-site prediction: pocket-based classifiers (Allosite SVM, random forest) that ignore communication, versus perturbation-response methods dominated by normal mode analysis of elastic network models (PARS), sometimes combined with machine learning (AlloPred, AllositePro), and the statistical-mechanical SBSMMA.
quote: Most available methods include NMA of ENM as the main component and use a perturbation approach to measure the response of the protein to ligand binding or unbinding, 36 thereby predicting allosteric sites, such as PARS.

claim: Stated limitation of the ENM/SBSMMA family that the atomistic graph avoids: they give no atomistic detail and ignore interactions beyond a cutoff distance (SBSMMA uses C-alpha contacts within 11 Angstrom).
quote: Although both ENM and SBSMMA are successful in modeling proteins and require much less computational power than MD simulations, they have two inherent limitations: not providing atomistic details of the protein and not considering long-range interactions greater than a certain distance.

claim: Concrete algorithm: the edge-to-edge transfer matrix is M = (1/2) W B^T L^dagger B with B the n x m incidence matrix of the atomistic graph, W the diagonal matrix of bond energies and L^dagger the pseudo-inverse of the weighted graph Laplacian.
quote: M is given by (Equation 1) M = 1 2 W B T L † B where B is the n × m incidence matrix for the atomistic protein graph with n nodes and m edges

claim: Failure mode relevant to seeding: in large multimeric proteins allosteric signal is only detected when enough orthosteric sites are used as source, e.g. ATCase (dodecamer, six orthosteric sites) needs at least three orthosteric sites involved before allosteric behaviour is detected.
quote: it has been demonstrated with ATCase, a large dodecameric protein with six orthosteric sites, that only when at least three orthosteric sites are involved is allosteric behavior detected.
